nutshell: Text-to-image person ReID needs large captioned datasets, but manual captioning is expensive and MLLM-generated captions are stylistically homogeneous even when prompted with hand-designed templates (existing work uses only 46-456 templates). HAM instead extracts a 'style' feature from each human-written caption (after neutralizing identity-specific attribute words), clusters these style features, and trains one learnable prompt per cluster so a frozen MLLM can mimic thousands of distinct human annotator styles; a complementary Uniform Prototype Sampling (UPS) method fixes standard clustering's tendency to under-represent sparse regions of the style space.
contributions: HAM: a pipeline that extracts identity-neutralized 'style' features from human captions (LLM-rewritten attribute words, encoded with a frozen CLIP text encoder), clusters them, and fine-tunes one learnable prompt per cluster (plus a small vision-language adaptor, with the MLLM itself frozen) so the MLLM can be conditioned to mimic K1 distinct human-annotator description styles rather than a small fixed set of hand-designed templates.

Uniform Prototype Sampling (UPS): because KMeans/DBSCAN concentrate cluster centers in dense regions of style-feature space, UPS instead defines a style feature space from the dataset's mean/std and uniformly samples K2 cluster centers within it, assigning the nearest Q samples to each (a sample can belong to multiple clusters or none) - producing clusters that cover sparse/rare style regions KMeans misses; combining KMeans+UPS gives the best ablation results.

HAM-PEDES: a 1M-image auto-captioned text-to-image ReID dataset (SYNTH-PEDES images + LLaVA1.6 captions via HAM) that sets new SOTA in both direct-transfer and fine-tuning settings against existing large-scale pretraining datasets (MALS, LUPerson-T, LUPerson-MLLM, SYNTH-PEDES), despite using fewer captions per image (2.0) than some competitors (2.53-4.0).
deficiencies: The paper's own 'extreme' template baseline - expanding to 68,126 hand-derived templates (row 3 in Table 1) - still only reaches R1=43.06/mAP=39.75 on CUHK-PEDES, far below HAM+UPS's 59.05/52.92 (row 8) despite using far more distinct 'styles' (68K templates vs. 1,000 clusters). The paper attributes this to 'style information lost in the manually designed process,' but the comparison also changes multiple other things at once (adaptor fine-tuning, prompt-based vs. hard-template conditioning), so the causal claim that clustering-plus-prompt-learning specifically is what matters isn't cleanly isolated.

UPS's own ablation shows an unexplained inconsistency: DBSCAN alone (row 7) is the worst clustering method tested (44.25 mAP on CUHK-PEDES with LLaVA), yet combining it with UPS (row 9: HAM+DBSCAN+UPS) is essentially tied with or slightly below UPS alone (row 8: 52.92 vs. 51.46 mAP) rather than clearly better or worse - the paper reports this row without discussing why adding a method it calls 'unsuitable for HAM' doesn't move the needle in a consistent direction.

The entire style-feature space depends on an LLM (Qwen2.5-7B) correctly identifying and neutralizing pedestrian-attribute words in human captions while preserving stylistic markers; if this intermediate rewriting step has systematic errors (over-neutralizing distinctive phrasing, missing attribute words), it would directly corrupt the clustering and UPS machinery built on top of it, but no validation of this step's quality (human spot-check, agreement rate, error analysis) is reported anywhere.

The paper reports pre-training data scaling only up to 1.0M images (Fig. 3) despite drawing from a 4.7M-image source pool (SYNTH-PEDES), with results showing steady improvement all the way to 1.0M - the paper doesn't explain why scaling wasn't pushed further, leaving the 'how far does this generalize' question about the method's core motivating claim (generalizability) open.
notable: The genuinely distinctive mechanical idea in UPS is that it deliberately abandons the standard clustering assumption that every sample belongs to exactly one cluster: nearest-Q assignment around uniformly-sampled centers (Eq. 5) means a caption can belong to multiple clusters or to none at all, which is what lets UPS place cluster centers in genuinely undersampled regions of style space instead of wherever samples happen to be dense. This 'assignment without exhaustive partition' pattern could be reusable for other diversity-injection problems beyond captioning style, wherever a diverse representative set matters more than a complete partition of the data.
